title: The Overtime Multiplier: Why an Extra Trading Hour Before Christmas Rarely Pays for Itself
excerpt: Extending trading hours into December feels like straightforward extra revenue. Once penalty rates and casual loading are counted properly, the margin on those extra hours is often far thinner than owners assume.
content:
Christmas trading brings an obvious temptation: stay open later, add a Sunday shift, push the closing time back an hour through December. The logic feels sound. More hours open means more chances to sell, and more chances to sell means more revenue landing before the year closes.

What gets skipped is the second half of that sentence. More revenue is not automatically more profit, and the hour added onto the end of a trading day or carved out of a Sunday roster rarely costs the same as the hours already on the books. It usually costs more, sometimes by enough that the extra trading barely breaks even once the wage bill for that specific hour is properly tallied.

This is the calculation that is easy to skip in the rush of November, when the focus is on getting the roster filled and the doors open rather than on what each extra hour actually contributes once the full cost of staffing it is counted.

Why the Marginal Hour Costs More Than the Average One

The wage cost of a normal Tuesday afternoon shift and the wage cost of a Sunday evening shift in the same week are rarely the same number, even though both might show up as plain "wages" on the same line of the profit and loss. Evening, weekend and public holiday loadings under many retail and hospitality awards can lift the hourly rate well above the rate paid during standard trading hours, and a shift worked on a public holiday such as Boxing Day can cost close to double the base rate before any other on-costs are added.

Bringing on extra casual staff to cover the surge adds a further layer. Casual loading sits on top of the base rate to begin with, and a new casual team member, however capable, typically needs several shifts to reach the same sales-per-hour or table-turn rate as an experienced staff member. The business pays a premium rate for a lower output in those early shifts, at precisely the point in the calendar when every hour is meant to be carrying its full share of the quarter's result.

The Comparison Most Owners Skip Before Adding the Shift

The test that actually answers whether an extra trading hour is worth running is simple, even if it rarely gets done before the roster is locked in. Take the extra revenue that hour is realistically expected to generate, apply the normal gross margin to find the extra profit dollar, then subtract the full wage cost of staffing that hour, loadings and all, plus the superannuation sitting on top. What remains is the hour's true contribution, not the revenue it generates.

On a 40 percent gross margin, an hour that brings in $400 in extra sales contributes $160 in gross profit before labour is counted. If staffing that hour costs $55 once penalty rates, casual loading and superannuation are included, the hour still clears $105. Move the same hour onto a public holiday, where the loaded wage cost might run closer to $90, and the contribution nearly halves. Run the same arithmetic on a leaner 25 percent margin and a public holiday shift can tip into contributing almost nothing at all, even while the till is ringing all afternoon.

When the Extra Hours Are Genuinely Worth Running

None of this is an argument against trading longer over the Christmas peak. Plenty of businesses capture real, incremental demand by opening earlier, staying open later or trading on a day they normally close, particularly where customers are shopping specifically because of the extended hours rather than simply shifting the same visit to a different time of day.

The distinction worth drawing before the roster is set is between hours that create new demand and hours that simply move existing demand around the clock. An extra Thursday evening that pulls in shoppers who would not otherwise have come in on Saturday is worth the loaded wage cost. An extra Sunday that mostly draws the same customers who would have shopped on Friday is not adding revenue. It is adding labour cost against revenue that was coming regardless.

Working this out properly, hour by hour and shift by shift rather than as a single gut feel about "the Christmas period," is exactly the kind of exercise a Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review is built to run, comparing actual rostered cost against actual revenue by shift to show which hours are genuinely paying for themselves and which are quietly eating into the result. Retailers and hospitality venues across Queensland locking in their December rosters this week would do well to run the numbers before the shifts go live rather than after the quarter closes. For owners who want a second set of eyes on the full rostering and margin picture through the peak, that is the kind of question a fractional CFO is there to help answer.

faqs.q: Does trading longer hours over Christmas always increase overall profit?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Extra trading hours only lift profit if the revenue they bring in exceeds the full cost of staffing them, including any evening, weekend or public holiday loadings and casual on-costs. Many extended shifts generate genuine new revenue and are well worth running. Others simply move existing customers to a different time of day, which adds labour cost without adding sales, so the hour ends up contributing little or nothing to the result.

faqs.q: How much do penalty rates actually add to the cost of a Christmas trading shift?
faqs.a: It depends on the award and the day, but evening, weekend and especially public holiday loadings can be substantial. A shift worked on a day such as Boxing Day can cost close to double the standard hourly rate once the applicable loading is applied, before superannuation is added on top. That gap is easy to underestimate when a roster is being filled quickly in November and December.

faqs.q: What is the simplest way to test if an extra trading hour is worth running?
faqs.a: Estimate the extra revenue the hour will realistically generate, apply your normal gross margin to find the extra profit dollar, then subtract the full loaded wage cost of staffing that hour. What is left is the hour's true contribution. Running this calculation before the roster is locked in, rather than reviewing results after the quarter closes, is the difference between a considered trading decision and a guess.

faqs.q: Should a small business use permanent staff or casuals for the Christmas trading surge?
faqs.a: Either can work, and the right mix depends on how long the surge in hours lasts and how quickly a new team member reaches full productivity. Casual staff carry a loading on top of the base rate and typically need several shifts to match an experienced staff member's output, so the early shifts of a casual's roster often cost more per dollar of revenue generated than an existing team member working the same hours.

faqs.q: How does a Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review help with Christmas rostering decisions?
faqs.a: A Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review compares actual rostered labour cost against actual revenue, shift by shift, to show which trading hours are genuinely profitable and which are quietly running at a loss once loadings and on-costs are counted. For a business adding hours through December, that comparison is the difference between extending trading with confidence and discovering the result in January.

faqs.q: What should Queensland retailers weigh up before extending December trading hours?
faqs.a: Retailers and hospitality venues across Queensland locking in longer December hours should weigh the loaded wage cost of each extra shift, including any public holiday loadings around Boxing Day and New Year, against the genuinely new revenue that shift is likely to bring in. The calculation takes an afternoon to run properly and is far cheaper than finding out the answer once the quarter's results are in.

faqs.q: How does a fractional CFO help a business decide which trading hours to keep?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO brings the discipline of running the contribution calculation across every shift and trading day, rather than relying on a general sense of how the Christmas period went. That turns next year's rostering decision into one based on actual shift-level numbers rather than a repeat of whatever was done the year before.
